area: Area I. Pilot Privileges and Currency
objective: By the end of this lesson you can list the documents you must have with you for any flight, say who may ask to see them, and give the deadlines for the two notices you owe the FAA: a change of address and a motor vehicle action.
why: A missing certificate, a forgotten ID or a move you never reported can ground you on the ramp, even when you are current and proficient. A late motor vehicle report can cost you the certificate itself.

prereading.what: The documents you must have when you act as a required pilot, photo ID, medical documents, and who may ask to inspect them (61.3(l)).
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.3

prereading.what: Alcohol and drug offenses, motor vehicle actions and the 60-day report, refusal to test, temporary certificates and how long certificates last.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.15 to 61.19

prereading.what: Replacing a lost certificate and the 60-day temporary authority document.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.29

prereading.what: Presenting your logbook on request, and which pilots must carry it.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.51(i)

prereading.what: English language standard at flight reviews and IPCs, and sending FAA Form 8710-1 so the FAA keeps a record of your time.
prereading.label: AC 61-98E 1.8 to 1.10, pp 1-3 to 1-5

prereading.what: The FAA Aviation English Language Standard and the "English Proficient" endorsement on your certificate.
prereading.label: AC 60-28B paragraphs 1 to 6.5, pp 1-5

warmup: Empty your pockets and flight bag in your head. If an FAA inspector met you at the airplane right now, which three documents could you hand over, and is the address on your certificate still where you live?

key_terms.def: The term 61.3(a) and (c) use for the pilots who must have the documents. It includes the PIC.
Where 61.3 lets you keep your documents if they are not on your person: in the aircraft you are flying.
Paper certificate issued after a checkride, good for up to 120 days until the permanent one arrives (61.17).
FAA document you may carry for up to 60 days in place of a lost certificate while a duplicate is on its way (61.29(e)).
One of the IDs listed in 61.3(a)(2), such as a driver's license, government ID, military ID, passport or SIDA badge.
A DUI-type conviction, or a driver's license suspension, revocation, cancellation or denial for an alcohol or drug cause (61.15(c)).
The address the FAA has for you. A change must be reported in writing within 30 days (61.60).
Security Identification Display Area: an airport area that needs a badge issued under 49 CFR part 1542.
Endorsement on a pilot certificate showing you met at least ICAO Operational Level 4 English (AC 60-28B).

chunks.title: What you must have with you

body.p: 14 CFR 61.3(a) applies to anyone who serves as a required pilot flight crewmember of a U.S. civil aircraft [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]]. That includes you as PIC.
When you exercise your privileges, each of these must be in your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft:

head: Document
Rule
What counts
rows: Pilot certificate
Your certificate, a temporary certificate, or a temporary authority document (next chunk)
Photo ID
Driver's license, government ID, military ID, passport, SIDA badge [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)(v)-(vi)]]
Medical
The right part 67 medical certificate, or other documentation acceptable to the FAA
Flight instructor certificate (if instructing)
Your CFI certificate or other documentation acceptable to the FAA

callout.text: Common mistake: leaving the certificate in the car, the hotel or the crew room. The rule says "physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft" [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]]. If it is not on you or in the airplane you are flying, you do not meet it.

body.p: Flying simulated instrument? 91.109(c)(1) says no person may do it unless the other control seat is occupied by a safety pilot who has at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]]. You log that safety pilot's name [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(1)(v)]].

callout.text: Common mistake: forgetting that the safety pilot needs documents too. 91.109(c)(1) requires a safety pilot with at least a private certificate and category and class ratings for the aircraft [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]]. The FAA treats that safety pilot as a required pilot flightcrew member, so the safety pilot must hold a medical certificate [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]], and 61.3's document rules apply [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]]. BasicMed now also covers serving as a required flightcrew member [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]].

check.q: You are PIC. Your certificate is in your car in the airport lot, and you plan to stay in the pattern. Do you meet 61.3?
check.a: No. It must be in your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft, not in the car [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]].

body.p: 61.3(a)(1) lists what you may carry as your pilot certificate [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]]:

bullets: A pilot certificate issued under part 61 [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)(i)]].
A temporary certificate under 61.17 [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)(iii)]].
A temporary authority document from the Airmen Certification Branch under 61.29(e) [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)(iv)]].
On a flight in the United States for a part 121 or 135 operator, a temporary document from that operator under its approved certificate verification plan [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)(v)]].
Also listed: a special purpose pilot authorization, a fractional program manager's document, and a foreign license when flying in that country [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]].

head: Document
How long it is good
rows: Pilot certificate
No expiration date. Valid unless surrendered, suspended or revoked [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(a)(2), (c)(1)]]
Temporary certificate
Issued for up to 120 days. Ends on the date shown, when the permanent one arrives, or on notice of denial or revocation [[60:203|14 CFR 61.17]]
Temporary authority after a loss
Up to 60 days while you wait for the duplicate, unless you are told the certificate was suspended or revoked [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)(1)]]

body.p: License No. 1 had an expiration date printed on it: April 6th, 1928 [[1:20|PHAK 1-5]]. Your pilot certificate today is issued without one [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(c)(1)]]. What runs out is your medical, your flight review and your currency.

Your ratings matter too. To act as PIC under IFR or in weather below VFR minimums, you need the category, class and instrument rating on your pilot certificate [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)(1)]], or an ATP certificate with the right category and class [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)(2)]].

callout.text: Changed: flight instructor certificates issued on or after December 1, 2024 have no expiration date. A CFI certificate issued before then still expires 24 calendar months from the month it was issued, renewed or reinstated [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(d)]].

body.p: Lost your certificate? Ask for a replacement by letter to the Airmen Certification Branch with the fee, or online through Airmen Services [[60:211|14 CFR 61.29(a)]]. The request gives your name, permanent mailing address, date and place of birth, and the grade, number and issue date of your certificate if you know them [[60:211|14 CFR 61.29(d)]]. Then ask for a temporary authority document. That request must include the date you asked for the duplicate [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)(2)]].

check.q: You passed your commercial checkride 100 days ago and the plastic certificate has not come. Is the temporary still good?
check.a: Only if its expiration date has not passed. It is issued for up to 120 days and ends on the date shown, when the permanent arrives, or on a denial or revocation notice [[60:203|14 CFR 61.17]].

body.p: You also need a photo ID in your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft. It must be one of these [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]] [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)(v)-(vi)]]:

bullets: Driver's license issued by a State, D.C., or a U.S. territory or possession.
Government ID card issued by the Federal government, a State, D.C., or a U.S. territory or possession.
U.S. Armed Forces ID card.
Official passport.
A credential for unescorted access to a SIDA at an airport regulated under 49 CFR part 1542.
Another form of ID the FAA finds acceptable.

body.p: A SIDA is a limited-access area that needs a badge issued under 49 CFR part 1542. You may not move into or through one without authorization and your ID on display [[33:173|AIM 2-3-15a]]. Pilots or passengers seen entering a SIDA without proper ID may be reported to TSA [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15b]].

callout.text: Common mistake: thinking your pilot certificate or medical is your ID. 61.3 requires a photo ID from the list in addition to the certificate and the medical [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)-(2)]].
BasicMed pilots: a passport works as photo ID, but it can't take the place of the U.S. driver's license that BasicMed needs [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

check.q: Your airport issued you a SIDA badge under 49 CFR part 1542. Can it serve as your 61.3 photo ID?
check.a: Yes. A credential for unescorted SIDA access at a part 1542 airport is on the list [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)(v)]].

body.p: To serve as a required pilot you must hold the right medical certificate, or other documentation acceptable to the FAA, in your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]. Which class you need is covered in the medical lesson (RF.I.C).

head: How you fly
Medical document you need
rows: With an FAA medical
Your part 67 medical certificate [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]
Under BasicMed

Hold and possess a U.S. driver's license [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(v)]] [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(xiii)]]. Have the completed medical examination checklist (CMEC) and the course completion certificate available in your logbook [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]]
CFI, not PIC and not a required pilot
No medical needed [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(viii)]], but carry your CFI certificate [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(d)(1)]]
CFI acting as PIC or required pilot
A medical, or BasicMed with a U.S. driver's license [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(xiv)]]

body.p: Under BasicMed, any restriction on your driver's license (glasses, daylight driving only and so on) applies in the airplane too [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]] [[36:10|AC 68-1A 4.2]]. If your license is revoked, you can't use BasicMed until it is reinstated [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

callout.text: Changed: the BasicMed aircraft limits are bigger than AC 68-1A says. 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) now allows an aircraft authorized for up to 7 occupants, up to 12,500 lb maximum takeoff weight, with up to 6 passengers [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]. AC 68-1A (2017) still lists 6 occupants, 6,000 lb and 5 passengers [[36:8|AC 68-1A 3.2]]. Follow the regulation.

check.q: You fly under BasicMed. What medical documents must be with you or in your logbook?
check.a: Your U.S. driver's license with you [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(v)]], and the CMEC and course completion certificate available in your logbook [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]].

chunks.title: Your logbook: what you record and when you carry it

body.p: You must record, in a manner acceptable to the FAA, the training and experience you use for a certificate, a rating or a flight review, and the experience you use for recent flight experience [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(a)]]. Each entry shows the date, total time, where you departed and arrived, the aircraft type and ID, and the safety pilot's name if 91.109 requires one [[60:227|14 CFR 61.51(b)(1)]].

head: Pilot
Must carry
rows: Student pilot, solo cross-country
Logbook, student pilot certificate and any other required record [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(2)]]
Sport pilot
Logbook or other evidence of required endorsements, on all flights [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(3)]]
Recreational pilot
Logbook with endorsements on certain solo flights, such as beyond 50 NM or at night [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(4)]]
Private, commercial, ATP
No carry rule, but you must present the logbook on a reasonable request [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]]

body.p: Endorsements are written and signed by an authorized person, usually a CFI [[1:31|PHAK 1-16]]. Keep flight review and IPC endorsements where you can find them.

callout.text: After a flight review or IPC, the FAA encourages your instructor to send FAA Form 8710-1 (best through IACRA). It is optional, but if you ever lose your logbook, the FAA then has a record on file [[15:8|AC 61-98E 1.10.2]].

check.q: As a commercial pilot, must you carry your logbook on a cross-country?
check.a: No carry rule applies to you, but you must present it on a reasonable request by the FAA, the NTSB or law enforcement [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

chunks.title: When someone asks to see them

body.p: 61.3(l) says you must present your airman certificate, medical certificate, BasicMed (part 68) documents, authorization or license, together with your photo ID, when one of these asks [[60:193|14 CFR 61.3(l)]] [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(3)-(4)]]. Your logbook and other part 61 records fall under 61.51(i)(1), which uses a slightly different list [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

head: Who asks
Certificate, medical and photo ID (61.3(l))
Logbook and records (61.51(i)(1))
rows: The FAA (Administrator)
Yes
Yes, on a reasonable request
An authorized NTSB representative
Yes
Yes, on a reasonable request
Any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer
Yes
Yes, on a reasonable request
An authorized TSA representative
Not on the 61.51(i)(1) list

body.p: The AIM adds that TSA's own rule, 49 CFR 1540, requires anyone holding an FAA airman certificate, medical certificate, authorization or license to present it on request from TSA [[33:174|AIM 2-3-15b]].

callout.text: Common mistake: thinking only the FAA can ask. A local police officer or a TSA representative may ask to see your certificate and photo ID, and you must show them [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(3)-(4)]].
Common mistake: thinking a BasicMed pilot has no medical paperwork to show. Documents that establish alternative medical qualification under part 68 are on the 61.3(l) list [[60:193|14 CFR 61.3(l)]].

check.q: A TSA representative at the FBO asks to see your pilot certificate. What must you show?
check.a: Your pilot certificate and your photo ID [[60:193|14 CFR 61.3(l)]] [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(4)]].

body.p: A certificate holder should be able to communicate in English with ATC, other pilots and others involved in preparing and flying the aircraft, with or without a radio [[10:1|AC 60-28B 1.1]]. Part 61 requires pilots to read, write, speak and understand English [[10:3|AC 60-28B 5.3.1]].

An "English Proficient" endorsement on a private, commercial or ATP certificate shows the holder was evaluated at the equivalent of at least ICAO Operational Level 4 [[10:5|AC 60-28B 6.4]]. Unless the FAA authorizes otherwise, no person may exercise certificate privileges without meeting the standard [[10:5|AC 60-28B 6.5]].

bullets: Your flight review or IPC instructor should evaluate your English throughout [[15:6|AC 61-98E 1.8.2]] [[10:4|AC 60-28B 6]].
If the instructor finds you don't meet the standard, they should not sign off the review. They log the training given and notify the Flight Standards office [[15:6|AC 61-98E 1.8.3]].
Only an FAA aviation safety inspector makes the final call [[15:6|AC 61-98E 1.8.4]].
For the English standard, a limitation is given only when the cause is medical, such as being unable to hear or speak. Weak English does not get a limitation [[10:7|AC 60-28B A.2.1.3]].

callout.text: All endorsements and records of training and checking in your logbook are entered in English [[10:1|AC 60-28B 3]].

check.q: During your flight review, who makes the final decision on whether you meet the English standard?
check.a: An FAA aviation safety inspector. The instructor refers you to the Flight Standards office [[15:6|AC 61-98E 1.8.4]].

chunks.title: Notice 1: change of address within 30 days

callout.text: 61.60: "The holder of a pilot, flight instructor, or ground instructor certificate who has made a change in permanent mailing address may not, after 30 days from that date, exercise the privileges of the certificate unless the holder has notified in writing the FAA, Airman Certification Branch, P.O. Box 25082, Oklahoma City, OK 73125, of the new permanent mailing address, or if the permanent mailing address includes a post office box number, then the holder's current residential address." [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]]

bullets: The clock starts on the date your permanent mailing address changes [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].
After day 30, without the written notice, you may not use the certificate at all: no PIC, no instructing [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].
If your new mailing address includes a P.O. box, the notice must give your current residential address [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].
It covers pilot, flight instructor and ground instructor certificates [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

body.p: Your address also shows up in other FAA paperwork: a replacement request lists your permanent mailing address [[60:211|14 CFR 61.29(d)(2)]], and a motor vehicle report includes your address [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)(1)]].

callout.text: Common mistake: updating your driver's license with the State and thinking the FAA knows. 61.60 needs written notice to the FAA Airman Certification Branch [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].
Move: 30 days. Motor vehicle action: 60 days.

check.q: You moved on June 10 and sent nothing to the FAA. Can you act as PIC on July 15?
check.a: No. More than 30 days have passed, so you may not exercise your privileges until you notify the FAA in writing [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

chunks.title: Notice 2: motor vehicle actions within 60 days

body.p: A motor vehicle action is any of these, after November 29, 1990 [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(c)]]:

bullets: A conviction under a Federal or State law for driving while intoxicated, impaired or under the influence of alcohol or a drug.
Cancellation, suspension or revocation of your driver's license for a cause related to driving while intoxicated, impaired or under the influence.
Denial of a driver's license application for that kind of cause.

body.p: You must send a written report of each motor vehicle action to the FAA Civil Aviation Security Division (AMC-700), P.O. Box 25810, Oklahoma City, OK 73125, no later than 60 days after the action [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]]. The report includes:

bullets: Your name, address, date of birth and airman certificate number.
The type of violation.
The date of the conviction or administrative action.
The State that holds the record.
Whether it came from the same incident as a motor vehicle action you already reported [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)(1)-(5)]].

head: Event
Can lead to
rows: Not sending the 60-day report
Denial of an application for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(f)]]
Two motor vehicle actions within 3 years (not from the same incident)
Denial for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(d)]]
Drug conviction (growing, sale, possession and so on)
Denial for up to 1 year after conviction, or suspension or revocation [[60:201|14 CFR 61.15(a)]]
An act banned by 91.17(a) or 91.19(a) (alcohol or drugs in flight)
Denial for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation [[60:201|14 CFR 61.15(b)]] [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(b)(1)-(2)]]
Refusing an alcohol test or release of results under 91.17(c) or (d)
Denial for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.16]] [[60:203|14 CFR 61.16(a)-(b)]]

callout.text: Common mistake: reporting only the court conviction. A license suspension for the same arrest is its own motor vehicle action. Report each one within 60 days of that action and say whether it came from the same incident [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(c), (e)]].

check.q: Your State suspends your driver's license for a DUI-related cause on April 1. The court convicts you on May 20. How many reports, and by when?
check.a: Two. Report the suspension within 60 days of April 1 and the conviction within 60 days of May 20, noting that they came from the same incident [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(c), (e)]].

chunks.title: Risk: an electronic copy or an old address

body.p: The trap is believing that "close enough" counts. A photo of your certificate on your phone is not on the 61.3(a)(1) list [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]]. The FAA's way to cover a lost certificate is the temporary authority document, good for up to 60 days [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)]].

The same goes for ID. A picture of your driver's license is not one of the IDs listed in 61.3(a)(2) [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]]. And under BasicMed you must hold and possess the license itself [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(v)]].

An old address is a quiet trap. Nothing stops the airplane from starting, but after 30 days without written notice you may not exercise your privileges [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]]. Any flight you fly as PIC after that is outside your certificate.

head: Hazard
How to manage it
rows: Certificate left at home or lost

Keep certificate, medical and photo ID together in one place you check before every flight. If lost, request a duplicate and a temporary authority document [[60:211|14 CFR 61.29(a)]] [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)]]
Relying on a phone photo
Carry the real documents. Only the listed documents count [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]]
Moving and forgetting the FAA
Put the written FAA notice on your moving checklist, due within 30 days [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]]
A DUI arrest that "isn't a conviction yet"
A license suspension counts on its own. Report within 60 days [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(c)(2), (e)]]

callout.text: AC 61-98E says a flight review should include changes to the operating rules, and a pilot who has not flown in years may need a fuller review of part 91 [[15:25|AC 61-98E 4.2.2-4.2.3]]. Ask your instructor to include a quick document check.

check.q: Your certificate is lost. Your friend says a clear photo of it on your phone is fine for a few weeks. Is it?
check.a: No. A photo is not on the 61.3(a)(1) list. Request a duplicate and a temporary authority document, which you may carry for up to 60 days [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]] [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)]].

chunks.title: Check it step by step: documents and notices

body.p: Run this before any flight where you are PIC or a required pilot:

bullets: Certificate: the plastic one, or a temporary (under 120 days and not past its date) or a temporary authority document (up to 60 days) [[60:203|14 CFR 61.17]] [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)(1)]].
Ratings: the certificate shows the category, class and, for IFR, the instrument rating you need, or you hold an ATP with the right category and class [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)(1)-(2)]].
Photo ID from the 61.3(a)(2) list [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]].
Medical certificate, or under BasicMed your U.S. driver's license plus the CMEC and course certificate in your logbook [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]] [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]].
CFI certificate if you will instruct [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(d)(1)]].

Any other required pilot flight crewmember has the same documents [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]]. For hood work, the safety pilot holds at least a private certificate with the right category and class ratings [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]].
Notices: moved in the last 30 days? Written notice sent [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]]. Any motor vehicle action in the last 60 days? Report sent [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]].
Logbook where you can present it on a reasonable request [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

head: Common error
Fix
rows: Medical in the flight bag, bag in the car
Documents must be on you or in the aircraft [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]
Pilot certificate used as the photo ID
Carry a separate listed photo ID [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]]
Temporary certificate past its date
It has expired. Don't fly on it [[60:203|14 CFR 61.17(b)]]
Thinking TSA can't ask
TSA is on the 61.3(l) list [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(4)]]
Address change only at the DMV
Notify the FAA in writing within 30 days [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]]

check.q: Name the three documents every required pilot must have for a powered airplane flight with an FAA medical.
check.a: Pilot certificate, photo ID and medical certificate, each in physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]] [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]].

scenario.title: A lost certificate, a recent move and a ramp check
scenario.setup: You are a commercial pilot with an instrument rating and a current medical. Five weeks ago you moved across town. You updated your driver's license with the State but sent nothing to the FAA. On Saturday you plan to fly two friends to the coast in a rented Cessna 182. At the FBO you open your wallet: driver's license and medical are there, but the plastic pilot certificate is gone. You do have a clear photo of it on your phone. While you think it over, a State police officer working at the airport walks over and asks to see your pilot certificate.

questions.q: Can the photo on your phone stand in for the lost certificate?
questions.a: No. 61.3(a)(1) lists the documents that count, and a photo is not one of them [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]]. Request a duplicate [[60:211|14 CFR 61.29(a)]], then a temporary authority document, which you may carry for up to 60 days [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)]].

questions.q: Even with the certificate in hand, can you act as PIC today?
questions.a: No. You changed your permanent mailing address five weeks ago. After 30 days without written notice to the FAA Airman Certification Branch, you may not exercise your privileges [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]]. The DMV update does not count.

questions.q: Must you answer the State police officer's request, and what do you show?
questions.a: Yes. Any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer may ask. You show your photo ID and your medical, and explain that the certificate is lost [[60:193|14 CFR 61.3(l)]] [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(3)]].

questions.q: The officer then asks for your logbook, which is at home. Were you required to carry it?
questions.a: No. As a commercial pilot you have no carry rule, but you must present it on a reasonable request by law enforcement, so offer to show it [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

questions.q: One friend is a private pilot whose State suspended his driver's license 50 days ago after a DUI arrest. The court case is still open. What does he owe the FAA?
questions.a: The suspension is a motor vehicle action by itself, so he must send a written report to AMC-700 within 60 days, 10 days from now [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(c)(2), (e)]]. If a conviction follows, that is another action with its own 60-day report [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)(5)]].

skills.do: For a flight the instructor describes, list every document you and any other required pilot must have (certificate or allowed substitute, photo ID, medical or BasicMed documents, CFI certificate if instructing), say who may ask to inspect them, and state any address or motor vehicle notice you owe, with its deadline.
skills.practice: Before your next flight, lay out your documents and check each against 61.3 [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)]] [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]]. Then ask yourself: have I moved in the last 30 days [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]], or had a motor vehicle action in the last 60 [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]]? Ask your flight review instructor to quiz you on it [[15:25|AC 61-98E 4.2.3]].

quiz.q: When you act as PIC, where must your pilot certificate be?
options: Anywhere on the airport, such as your car
In your physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft
On file with the FBO that rents you the airplane
Only on cross-country flights, in your flight bag
quiz.why: 61.3(a)(1) says physical possession or readily accessible in the aircraft [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)]].

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an acceptable photo ID under 61.3(a)(2)?
options: An official passport
A U.S. Armed Forces ID card
Your FAA medical certificate
A State driver's license
quiz.why: The medical certificate is a separate required document, not one of the listed photo IDs [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]] [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(c)(1)]].

quiz.q: A temporary pilot certificate is issued for up to:
options: 30 days
60 days
90 days
120 days
quiz.why: 61.17(a): up to 120 days, until the permanent certificate is issued [[60:203|14 CFR 61.17(a)]].

quiz.q: After you lose your certificate, how long may you carry the FAA's temporary authority document?
options: Up to 60 days, pending the duplicate
Up to 120 days, like a temporary certificate
Until your next flight review
Up to 30 days
quiz.why: 61.29(e)(1): up to 60 days while you wait for the duplicate [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)(1)]].

quiz.q: You change your permanent mailing address. What does 61.60 require?
options: Tell your AME at your next medical
Notify the FAA in writing within 60 days
Notify the FAA Airman Certification Branch in writing; after 30 days you can't use the certificate until you do
Nothing, as long as the State has your new address
quiz.why: 61.60: after 30 days you may not exercise privileges unless you have notified the Airman Certification Branch in writing [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

quiz.q: How long do you have to report a motor vehicle action, and to whom?
options: 30 days, to the Airman Certification Branch
60 days, to the FAA Civil Aviation Security Division (AMC-700)
60 days, to your local Flight Standards office
Only at your next medical exam
quiz.why: 61.15(e): a written report to AMC-700 no later than 60 days after the action [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]].

quiz.q: Which of these is on the 61.3(l) list but NOT on the 61.51(i)(1) logbook list?
options: The FAA
An NTSB representative
A local police officer
A TSA representative
quiz.why: 61.3(l)(4) adds TSA for your certificate and ID [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(4)]]. 61.51(i)(1) names only the FAA, NTSB and law enforcement [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

quiz.q: Under BasicMed, which document must you hold and possess in place of a medical certificate?
options: Your passport
A U.S. driver's license
Your BasicMed course certificate
Your physician's business card
quiz.why: 61.23(c)(1)(v) requires a medical certificate or a U.S. driver's license [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(v)]]. A passport can't replace the license [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

quiz.q: During a flight review, your instructor decides you don't meet the English language standard. What should happen?
options: The instructor endorses a failed flight review
The instructor signs off the review and adds a limitation
The instructor logs the training given, doesn't sign off the review, and notifies the Flight Standards office
Nothing, because English is only checked on checkrides
quiz.why: No failure endorsement exists. The instructor logs training only and notifies Flight Standards [[15:6|AC 61-98E 1.8.3]].

takeaways: Every required pilot carries three things: certificate, photo ID, medical (or BasicMed driver's license), on you or in the aircraft.
Substitutes: temporary certificate up to 120 days, temporary authority after a loss up to 60 days. A phone photo is not one.
Show certificate and ID to the FAA, NTSB, law enforcement or TSA. Show the logbook on a reasonable request; TSA is not on that list.
Moved? Written notice to the FAA within 30 days, or you can't use the certificate.
Motor vehicle action? Written report to AMC-700 within 60 days, one for each action.
Changed: new CFI certificates don't expire, and BasicMed limits are now 7 occupants, 12,500 lb, 6 passengers.
cfi_notes: AC 68-1A 3.2 (2017) still lists BasicMed limits of 6 occupants, 6,000 lb and 5 passengers. Current 14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) allows 7 occupants, 12,500 lb and 6 passengers. Teach the regulation.

AC 68-1A 4.1 says BasicMed can't be used to fly as a safety pilot unless that pilot is PIC, but current 61.113(i) reads "act as pilot in command or serve as a required flightcrew member." Check the current rule with the student; the medical lesson (RF.I.C) goes deeper.
Students mix up the two inspection lists. 61.3(l) (certificate, medical, ID) includes TSA; 61.51(i)(1) (logbook) does not, and adds "reasonable request."
Airline pilots often rely on the company's certificate verification plan. 61.3(a)(1)(v) covers only flights for the part 121 or 135 operator inside the United States, not their weekend flying.
Ask "what is in your wallet right now?" at every flight review. Most pilots discover an old address or a CFI certificate they think still expires.
Stress that a license suspension and a later conviction from one DUI arrest are two motor vehicle actions, each with its own 60-day report (61.15(c), (e)).

The rule text of 91.109(c)(1) and 61.3 doesn't use the words "required pilot flightcrew member" for the safety pilot, but AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1 says it plainly: because a safety pilot is a required pilot flightcrew member, the safety pilot must hold a medical certificate [[36:14|AC 68-1A 5.2.2.1]]. Teach that, and note the AC's "PIC only" BasicMed limit is outdated by current 61.113(i) [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)]].
Many pilots remember 61.3 as "physical possession" only. The current text adds "or readily accessible in the aircraft"; it does not cover the car or the FBO.
gaps: The sources do not say whether a digital image of a certificate, or any FAA electronic certificate, is acceptable. The lesson teaches only the 61.3(a)(1) list and the 61.29(e) temporary authority document.
61.60 names written notice to the Airman Certification Branch. The sources do not describe an online address change process.
How motor vehicle actions are also reported on the FAA medical application (Form 8500-8) is not in the uploaded sources.
The sources say only that logbook records must be kept "in a manner acceptable to the Administrator"; they give no detail on electronic logbooks.
The text of 49 CFR 1540 (TSA) is not in the sources; the lesson uses the AIM 2-3-15 summary.

activities.title: Lost certificate: get back in the air
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Ask the Airmen Certification Branch for a duplicate, by letter with the fee or online through Airmen Services
Ask for a temporary authority document, giving the date you requested the duplicate
Carry the temporary authority document as your certificate when you fly
When the duplicate arrives, carry it in place of the temporary document
activities.why: The duplicate request comes first [[60:211|14 CFR 61.29(a)]]. The temporary authority request must include the date you asked for the duplicate, and you may carry that document for up to 60 days until the duplicate arrives [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)]].

activities.title: Is it a 61.3 photo ID?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: SIDA badge from a part 1542 airport

activities.why: The listed IDs are a driver's license, government ID, Armed Forces ID, passport, SIDA credential, or another form the FAA accepts [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)]] [[60:189|14 CFR 61.3(a)(2)(v)-(vi)]]. The certificate, medical and BasicMed papers are separate required documents [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]].

activities.title: Who carries what
activities.intro: Tap a pilot, then what that pilot must carry or have.

pairs.r: Logbook, student certificate and other required records
Logbook or endorsement evidence on all flights
No carry rule, but show it on reasonable request
CMEC and course certificate available in the logbook

activities.why: Carry rules are in 61.51(i)(1)-(4) [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)]]. BasicMed papers must be available in the logbook [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(3)]].

activities.title: True or false: who may ask?
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A TSA representative may ask to see your pilot certificate and photo ID.
cards.why: True. TSA is on the 61.3(l) list [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(4)]].

cards.s: 61.51(i)(1) lists TSA among those who may ask to see your logbook.
cards.why: False. 61.51(i)(1) names the FAA, the NTSB and law enforcement only [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

cards.s: A private pilot must carry the logbook on every flight.
cards.why: False. The carry rules cover student, sport, recreational and sport-rated instructors. Others present it on reasonable request [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)]].

cards.s: A county sheriff's deputy may ask to see your medical certificate.
cards.why: True. Any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer may ask [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(3)]].

cards.s: When you show your certificate on request, you must show your photo ID too.
cards.why: True. 61.3(l) says present it and your photo ID [[60:193|14 CFR 61.3(l)]].

cards.s: A BasicMed pilot has no medical documents that an inspector can ask for.
cards.why: False. Part 68 alternative medical documents are on the 61.3(l) list [[60:193|14 CFR 61.3(l)]].

activities.title: Which rule goes with which field?
activities.intro: Each card is a rule, not a field name. Drag each rule to the numbered pin on the field it is about.

pins.label: 61.60: written notice within 30 days of a change
61.19(c): nothing else is printed to end it
61.3(e)(1): IFR as PIC needs instrument airplane here
English: an entry here only for a medical cause
Private, commercial or ATP is printed here

activities.why: Pin 1, address: notify the FAA in writing within 30 days of a change in permanent mailing address [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]]. Pin 2, date of issue: a pilot certificate is issued without an expiration date [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(c)(1)]]. Pin 3, ratings: to act as PIC under IFR you need the instrument rating on your certificate [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)(1)]], unless you hold an ATP [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)(2)]]. Pin 4, limitations: for the English standard a limitation is given only for a medical cause, such as being unable to hear [[10:7|AC 60-28B A.2.1.3]]. Pin 5, grade (this sample says flight engineer): a replacement request asks for the grade of your certificate [[60:211|14 CFR 61.29(d)(4)(i)]].

activities.title: Count the days
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You moved on September 20 and have not notified the FAA. What is the last day in October you may still exercise your privileges (30 days after the move)?
items.why: September has 30 days: 10 days take you to September 30, and 20 more reach October 20. After that you may not use the certificate until you notify the FAA in writing [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

items.q: A court convicts you of a DUI on May 10. What is the last day in July your written report can be sent (60 days after)?
items.why: 21 days to May 31, 30 more to June 30 (51 days), 9 more to July 9 (60 days) [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(e)]].

items.q: Your certificate was lost and the FAA issued a temporary authority document on August 15. What is the last day in October you may carry it (60 days)?
items.why: 16 days to August 31, 30 more to September 30 (46 days), 14 more to October 14 (60 days) [[60:212|14 CFR 61.29(e)(1)]].

items.q: You passed a checkride on March 1 and got a temporary certificate. What is the latest day in June it can last (120 days)?
items.why: 30 days to March 31, 30 to April 30 (60), 31 to May 31 (91), 29 more to June 29 (120). It ends sooner if the date shown is earlier or the permanent one arrives [[60:203|14 CFR 61.17]].

activities.title: Can I fly today?
activities.intro: It is Saturday, October 17. You are an instrument-rated private pilot flying under BasicMed, with a current flight review and passenger currency. You plan a two-hour VFR trip with two friends in a club Cessna 172. You moved to a new apartment on October 1.

steps.s: Packing your flight bag, you realize you have not told the FAA about the move. What now?
options: Cancel: you may not fly at all after a move until the FAA updates your certificate
You may fly today, but get written notice to the Airman Certification Branch by October 31
Ignore it: updating your driver's license with the State is enough
You have 60 days, so it can wait until December
steps.why: October 1 plus 30 days is October 31, so today is inside the window. After that you may not exercise privileges without written notice [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

steps.s: At the airport you find your wallet with your driver's license is at home. You have your passport, certificate and logbook with the CMEC and course certificate. What do you do?
options: Fly: the passport is a valid photo ID
Fly: the CMEC in your logbook replaces the license
Go get the driver's license, or delay, because BasicMed needs it with you
Fly, and show a photo of the license if asked
steps.why: A passport is a valid photo ID, but under BasicMed you must hold and possess a U.S. driver's license, and a passport can't replace it [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(v)]] [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

steps.s: Back with your license, a county sheriff's deputy at the fuel pump asks to see your pilot certificate. What do you do?
options: Refuse: only the FAA may ask
Show the certificate and your photo ID
Show only the certificate
Ask the deputy to call the FAA first
steps.why: Any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer may ask, and you present the certificate with your photo ID [[60:193|14 CFR 61.3(l)]] [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(3)]].

steps.s: The deputy also asks for your logbook. It is in your flight bag. What is the right answer?
options: Show it: law enforcement may ask on a reasonable request
Refuse: private pilots don't have to carry a logbook
Show it only if a TSA representative is present
Show only the BasicMed pages
steps.why: You are not required to carry it, but on a reasonable request by law enforcement you must present it [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: You are an airline first officer on a part 121 trip inside the United States. Your plastic certificate was lost yesterday, and the airline gave you a temporary document under its approved certificate verification plan. May you fly the trip?
options: Yes, that document is on the 61.3(a)(1) list for this flight
No, only the plastic certificate counts
Yes, but only as a non-required crewmember
No, you need a 61.17 temporary certificate
final_quiz.why: 61.3(a)(1)(v) allows a temporary document from a part 121 or 135 operator under an approved certificate verification plan, for its flights within the United States [[60:188|14 CFR 61.3(a)(1)(v)]].

final_quiz.q: You are a CFI in the right seat with a rated private pilot who is acting as PIC. You are not PIC and not a required pilot. What must you have?
options: A medical and your CFI certificate
Nothing, since you are not PIC
Your CFI certificate; no medical is required
Only a photo ID
final_quiz.why: No medical is needed when the CFI is not PIC or a required pilot [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(c)(2)(viii)]], but the CFI certificate must be in possession or readily accessible [[60:190|14 CFR 61.3(d)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: You moved on September 1. It is October 5 and you have not written to the FAA. You are otherwise current. May you act as PIC today?
options: Yes, the deadline is 60 days
No, more than 30 days have passed without written notice
Yes, as long as your medical shows the new address
Yes, the rule only applies to instructors
final_quiz.why: After 30 days from the change, you may not exercise privileges until you notify the Airman Certification Branch in writing [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

final_quiz.q: Your new permanent mailing address is a P.O. box. What address must your 61.60 notice give?
options: Your employer's address
Your home airport's address
Your current residential address
Only the P.O. box
final_quiz.why: If the permanent mailing address includes a post office box number, the notice gives your current residential address [[60:245|14 CFR 61.60]].

final_quiz.q: After one DUI arrest, your State suspends your license on February 10 and a court convicts you on March 3. What do you owe the FAA?
options: One report within 60 days of the arrest
Two written reports, each within 60 days of its action, noting they came from the same incident
Nothing until your next medical
One report within 30 days of the conviction
final_quiz.why: Each suspension and conviction is a motor vehicle action. Report each no later than 60 days after it, and state whether it came from the same incident [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(c), (e)]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot has two motor vehicle actions from two separate incidents, 26 months apart. What does 61.15 allow the FAA to do?
options: Nothing, since each was reported on time
Only issue a warning letter
Deny an application for up to 1 year, or suspend or revoke certificates
Require a new checkride only
final_quiz.why: A motor vehicle action within 3 years of another (not from the same incident) is grounds for denial for up to 1 year or suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15(d)]].

final_quiz.q: Your temporary certificate from a checkride 130 days ago is in your wallet. The permanent card hasn't come. Can you fly on it?
options: Yes, temporaries last until the permanent arrives
Yes, for up to 180 days
Only with a passenger who is a CFI
No, it is issued for at most 120 days, so it has expired
final_quiz.why: A temporary is issued for up to 120 days and expires on the date shown [[60:203|14 CFR 61.17]]. Don't fly on it.

final_quiz.q: A BasicMed pilot left his driver's license at home but has his passport, certificate and logbook. Can he act as PIC?
options: Yes, the passport is a valid photo ID and medical document
No, BasicMed requires him to hold and possess a U.S. driver's license
Yes, the CMEC in the logbook covers it
Yes, if he flies solo
final_quiz.why: A pilot flying under 61.113(i) must hold and possess a U.S. driver's license or a medical certificate [[60:206|14 CFR 61.23(c)(1)(v)]]. A passport is a valid ID but can't replace the license [[36:9|AC 68-1A 4.2]].

final_quiz.q: At a fly-in, a city police officer asks to see your pilot certificate. What does the rule say?
options: You must present it and your photo ID
Only FAA inspectors may ask
You may refuse unless you are being arrested
You must present it only if the officer shows a warrant
final_quiz.why: 61.3(l)(3) includes any Federal, State or local law enforcement officer, and you present the certificate with your photo ID [[60:193|14 CFR 61.3(l)]] [[60:194|14 CFR 61.3(l)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: An FAA inspector asks to see your logbook after you land. You are a private pilot and the logbook is at home. What is true?
options: You violated 61.51 by not carrying it
You must present it on a reasonable request, but you were not required to carry it
You never have to show your logbook
Only the NTSB may ask for logbooks
final_quiz.why: Private pilots have no carry rule but must present the logbook on a reasonable request by the FAA [[60:231|14 CFR 61.51(i)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Your flight instructor certificate was issued in January 2025. When does it expire?
options: 24 calendar months after issue
It has no expiration date
When your medical expires
At your next flight review
final_quiz.why: CFI certificates issued on or after December 1, 2024 have no expiration date [[60:203|14 CFR 61.19(d)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Under BasicMed, may you act as PIC of a 7-seat airplane with an 8,000 lb maximum takeoff weight, carrying 6 passengers, VFR below 18,000 ft in the U.S.?
options: No, BasicMed is limited to 6,000 lb
No, BasicMed is limited to 5 passengers
Yes, it is within the 7 occupant, 12,500 lb and 6 passenger limits
No, BasicMed allows only 4 seats
final_quiz.why: 61.113(i)(1) allows up to 7 occupants, 12,500 lb and 6 passengers [[60:308|14 CFR 61.113(i)(1)]]. The 6,000 lb and 5 passenger numbers are from the older AC 68-1A [[36:8|AC 68-1A 3.2]].

final_quiz.q: Your instructor doubts a pilot's English during an IPC. Who decides whether the pilot meets the standard?
options: The instructor
Any designated pilot examiner
The local airport manager
An FAA aviation safety inspector, after referral to Flight Standards
final_quiz.why: Only an FAA ASI can make that determination; the instructor must refer the pilot to the Flight Standards office [[15:6|AC 61-98E 1.8.4]].

final_quiz.q: You plan hood work in a Cessna 172 with a friend as safety pilot. What does 91.109(c)(1) require of the pilot in the other control seat?
options: At least a private pilot certificate with airplane single-engine land ratings
An instrument rating
A flight instructor certificate
Only a current medical certificate
final_quiz.why: The other control seat must be occupied by a safety pilot with at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)(i)]]. The rule does not require an instrument rating or a CFI certificate.
